newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Cetes rates hit new post-crisis low.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Cetes rates hit new post-crisis low.

text.p: Mexico's bellwether one-month Cetes rate dropped on Tuesday to its lowest level since the peso crisis that started in late 1994.

At the central bank's primary auction, treasury bill rates fell more than expected on good liquidity in the secondary money market, a stable peso, strong demand and improving expectations for inflation, analysts said.
The one-month Cetes rate fell 102 basis points to 21.91 percent, down for the sixth week in a row after reaching 27.37 percent on December 17.
"This could be a 'market' drop due to the levels we saw in the secondary market," Banco Union analyst Ricardo Vazquez said.
Mexican overnight secondary Cetes rates closed at 21.25 percent on Tuesday.
"The strong demand and expectations for inflation also helped rates to drop," Vazquez said.
Demand was a strong 14.38 billion pesos, up from 12.72 billion pesos the week before.
A Reuters survey of nine money market dealers earlier in the day showed expectations of a decline of 53 basis points for the one-month Cetes.

Some analysts said the drop may have been steeper than expected because the one-month paper was assigned to only two bidders, and they speculated that local financial institutions may have placed the low bids to help keep interest rates on a downward trend.
"Levels of 21 percent were what we were expecting for the month of February, not now," said one analyst who declined to be identified.
The average rate on 28-day treasury bills was 20.07 percent in December 1994, but they rose as high as 74.84 percent in the month of April 1995.
The deep financial crisis caused rates to fluctuate widely.
While analysts expect rates to continue to fall, they see uncertainty again causing some volatility in Cetes auctions.

"April could be a relatively stable month for the fixed-income market and we believe that short-term rates could even drop further and break the 20 percent level for a couple of weeks," two economists with Santander Investment wrote in a recent report.
However, they noted, political campaigns before the key July 6 elections for Congressional seats and for several governorships could intensify political factors towards the end of May.
Analysts say the peso could weaken because of political uncertainty and if non-oil export growth slows, causing a bout of interest rate and exchange rate volatility.
Rates also dropped on longer-term Cetes this week, causing declines across the yield curve. ($1 = 7.8 pesos)
